title: Scottie Scheffler, Viktor Hovland to decide Travelers Championship with sudden-death playoff Monday
content:
Scottie Scheffler reminded us Sunday he feels the same way as the rest of us. He’s frustrated with not winning, too.

The world No. 1 has gone 12 starts without a victory, and when he sank a 9-foot par putt to force a playoff at the Travelers Championship, he let out an emotional fist pump and shout. He’s sick and tired of all those runners-up.

That putt sent Scheffler into a playoff with Norwegian fan favorite Viktor Hovland, but that sudden-death playoff will take place at 9 a.m. ET Monday as an 83-minute weather delay pushed Sunday’s finish into darkness.

They’ll play the 18th hole on repeat until one wins.

Scheffler led his playing partner, Hovland, by two shots when the weather delay halted play with five holes to go. When they returned, they found a practically new golf course soaked by the heavy rains. Collin Morikawa was already in the clubhouse at 20-under par, just one back of Scheffler.

But Hovland birdied the first two holes after the restart to meet Scheffler at 21-under. Meanwhile, on the short par four 15th, Scheffler hit a poor chip that shockingly sped past the wet greens and flew off the back. Scheffler held his hand over his mouth in absolute shock after the shot, and it took a difficult 8-foot par to maintain a share of the lead.

Then, on 17, with another chance to pull away, Scheffler’s birdie putt rolled off the edge for another disappointment. And on 18, Scheffler put his drive in heavy rough on a steep slope on the right of the fairway. It took an impressive shot to still land the green from there and save par.

It adds to what’s been a strange year for Scheffler. He remains the undeniable best player in the world, far above any peer in either the Official World Golf Ranking or the DataGolf rankings, but because of what he calls a lack of “sharpness,” he’s had a lot of close calls. After winning his first start this season at the American Express in January, Scheffler has gone 12 starts without a win.

In that time, he’s finished runner-up three times with seven top fives. Perhaps the discussion reached an apex last week at the U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills, where Scheffler shot a frustrating 71 playing in the final group as Wyndham Clark, the major’s winner, fell back to the field.

That fist pump showed the frustration Scheffler’s been feeling as he tries to get back into his usual place. Keep in mind, he won 16 times in 42 starts before this stretch. And to get over the hump, he’ll have to take down Hovland, the man who took the Tour Championship out of Scheffler’s grasp in 2023 but has fallen outside the top 20 in the three years since.
